Every option is a hydrogen electrode at 1 atm, so only the acid concentration differs.
For H⁺ + e⁻ ⇒ ½H₂ the Nernst equation gives
E = E° − 0.059 log(1/[H⁺]) = 0 + 0.059 log[H⁺]
So the sign of E follows the sign of log[H⁺]:
[H⁺] > 1 M ⇒ log positive ⇒ E > 0
[H⁺] = 1 M ⇒ log zero ⇒ E = 0, the standard hydrogen electrode by definition
[H⁺] < 1 M ⇒ log negative ⇒ E < 0
Check each: 1 M gives exactly zero; 0.1 M and 0.5 M are below 1 M and give negative values.
Only 2 M HCl has [H⁺] above 1 M.
E = 0.059 × log 2 = 0.059 × 0.301 = +0.018 V ✓
∴ Pt, ½H₂ (1 atm) | HCl (2 M).

kcet|Chemistry|2012|39||0|0.s:
Work backwards from ethanol, C₂H₅OH, which has two carbons.
Formaldehyde, HCHO, has only one. So the reagent must supply the second carbon, and that
points to a Grignard reagent.
CH₃MgI adds its methyl group to the carbonyl carbon:
HCHO + CH₃MgI ⇒ CH₃–CH₂–OMgI
Acid hydrolysis then protonates the alkoxide:
CH₃CH₂OMgI + H₂O/H⁺ ⇒ CH₃CH₂OH + Mg(OH)I
So X is CH₃MgI ✓
Note the general rule this illustrates: a Grignard with **formaldehyde** always gives a primary
alcohol with one more carbon; with any other aldehyde it gives a secondary alcohol, and with
a ketone a tertiary one.
The other reagents add no carbon at all — KOH and KCN would give a different functional
group entirely.
∴ CH₃MgI.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|40||0|0:
Basicity depends on how available the nitrogen lone pair is to accept a proton.
In **aniline**, C₆H₅NH₂, the nitrogen is attached directly to the benzene ring. Its lone pair
overlaps with the ring's π system and is delocalised into it, spread over the ortho and para
carbons. A lone pair that is busy being delocalised is not free to pick up a proton, so aniline
is a weak base.
In **benzylamine**, C₆H₅CH₂NH₂, there is a –CH₂– group between the nitrogen and the ring.
That sp³ carbon breaks the conjugation, so the nitrogen lone pair cannot reach the π system
and stays localised on nitrogen, fully available for protonation.
So benzylamine is the stronger base — its Kb is around 2 × 10⁻⁵ against aniline's 4 × 10⁻¹⁰,
a difference of some fifty thousand times.
(1) states the reverse of the truth and (3) denies the resonance that is the whole explanation.
∴ because the lone pair on the nitrogen of aniline is delocalised.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|41||0|0.s:
A methyl group releases electrons, destabilising the carboxylate anion, so on electronic
grounds a toluic acid should be **weaker** than benzoic acid. That holds for the para isomer.
p-Toluic acid < benzoic acid ✓
But the ortho isomer breaks the pattern. This is the **ortho effect**: any group next to the
–COOH, whether electron releasing or withdrawing, twists the carboxyl group out of the plane
of the ring. Once it is no longer coplanar, the carboxyl can no longer conjugate with the ring,
and that loss of resonance in the *acid* makes it easier to lose the proton.
Steric crowding also relieves itself when the planar COOH becomes the smaller COO⁻.
So o-toluic acid is **stronger** than benzoic acid despite its methyl group.
Putting them in decreasing order of acidity:
o-toluic acid > benzoic acid > p-toluic acid
∴ option (4).

kcet|Chemistry|2012|42||0|0:
Ethane is CH₃–CH₃. Each carbon forms four σ bonds — one to the other carbon and three to
hydrogens — and has no lone pair.
Four electron domains means four hybrid orbitals, so each carbon is **sp³** hybridised,
tetrahedral, with angles of 109°28′.
Now identify each overlap:
The C–C bond joins the two carbons, so it is an sp³ orbital on one meeting an sp³ orbital on the
other ⇒ **sp³–sp³**.
Each C–H bond joins a carbon to a hydrogen. Hydrogen has only its 1s orbital, so this is an sp³
orbital overlapping an s orbital ⇒ **sp³–s**.
Both are head-on overlaps along the internuclear axis, so both are σ bonds — which is why
ethane has free rotation about its C–C bond, there being no π bond to lock it.
∴ sp³–s and sp³–sp³.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|43||0|0.s:
The structure is CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₂–CO–CH₃.
Step 1 — choose the principal functional group. A ketone outranks an alcohol, so the compound
is named as a **pentanone** and the –OH becomes a 'hydroxy' prefix.
Step 2 — the chain has five carbons, so the parent is pentane ⇒ pentanone.
Step 3 — number to give the **ketone** the lower locant. Counting from the CH₃ nearest the
carbonyl:
C1 = CH₃
C2 = C=O
C3 = CH₂
C4 = CH–OH
C5 = CH₃
That puts the ketone at 2 and the hydroxyl at 4. Numbering from the other end would make
the ketone 4, which is higher and so not allowed.
Name: 4-hydroxypentan-2-one, written in the older style as 4-hydroxy-2-pentanone.
Option (3) wrongly names the ketone as 'oxo' while treating the alcohol as the parent, and
(2) numbers from the wrong end.
∴ 4-hydroxy-2-pentanone.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|44||0|0.s:
For a first order reaction,
k = (2.303/t)·log([A]₀/[A])
First find k from the data given. 60% complete means 40% remains:
k = (2.303/20)·log(100/40) = (2.303/20)·log 2.5
log 2.5 = 0.3979
k = (2.303 × 0.3979)/20 = 0.0458 min⁻¹
Now find the time for 84% completion, when 16% remains:
t = (2.303/k)·log(100/16)
log 6.25 = 0.7959
t = (2.303 × 0.7959)/0.0458 = 1.833/0.0458 = 40 min
There is a quicker route: 84% left as 16% is (40%)², so the fraction remaining has been
squared, which takes exactly twice the time — 2 × 20 = 40 min ✓
∴ 40 minutes.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|45||0|0.s:
Souring takes 5 hours at 27 °C and ten times longer, 50 hours, at −3 °C. Time is inversely
proportional to rate, so the rate at the higher temperature is 10 times the rate at the lower.
k₁/k₂ = 10
Convert the temperatures: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K, T₂ = −3 + 273 = 270 K.
Use the two-point Arrhenius equation:
log(k₁/k₂) = (Ea/2.303R)·(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)
1/270 − 1/300 = (300 − 270)/(270 × 300) = 30/81000 = 3.704 × 10⁻⁴
log 10 = 1, so
1 = (Ea/2.303R) × 3.704 × 10⁻⁴
Ea = 2.303R / (3.704 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.303 × R × 2700 J mol⁻¹
Expressed in kilojoules, 2700 J = 2.7 kJ:
Ea = 2.303 × 2.7 R kJ mol⁻¹
∴ 2.303 × 2.7 R kJ mol⁻¹.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|48||0|0:
Two conditions must both be met: the ligand must carry a negative charge, and it must bind
through **two** donor atoms.
(2) Cyano, CN⁻ — negatively charged ✓ but monodentate, donating only through carbon ✗
(3) Ethylenediamine, H₂N–CH₂CH₂–NH₂ — bidentate ✓ but **neutral**, not charged ✗
(4) Acetato, CH₃COO⁻ — negatively charged ✓, and usually binds through one oxygen only ✗
(1) Dimethylglyoximato — dimethylglyoxime loses one proton to give the anion, so it is
negatively charged ✓, and it chelates through the two nitrogen atoms of its oxime groups ✓
This is the ligand used to detect nickel: two of them close two five-membered rings around
Ni²⁺ to give the bright red, insoluble bis(dimethylglyoximato)nickel(II).
∴ dimethyl glyoximato.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|49||0|0.s:
In Werner's language, the **primary** valency is the oxidation state, satisfied by the ions
outside the coordination sphere, while the **secondary** valency is the coordination number —
the number of donor atoms attached directly to the metal.
Write the formula of tetraammine dichloroplatinum(IV) chloride:
[Pt(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl₂
Count the ligands inside the square brackets:
4 NH₃, each donating through nitrogen = 4
2 Cl⁻, each donating through chlorine = 2
total = 6
So the secondary valency is 6, and the geometry is octahedral.
The primary valency is +4, which is what options (1) and (2) are testing — the two chlorides
outside the bracket satisfy part of it.
Note the two chlorines *inside* the sphere count towards the coordination number but are not
ionisable.
∴ 6.
